prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the claims-triage agent (home and motor claims assessment within delegated authority) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: rebuild cost after an extension. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 1)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When a home has had an extension, I treat the original sum insured as a prompt to check whether the rebuild cost was reviewed after the works, because many policies only stay accurate if the extension was declared and the building sum adjusted."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the extension changed the footprint, height, or roofline, I look for evidence that the rebuild cost should include the whole property at current materials and labour rates, not just the new rooms on their own."},{"type":"observation","content":"When plans or completion paperwork are available, I use them to spot whether the extension added higher-cost features such as vaulted ceilings, bi-fold doors, or a larger kitchen, as these can push rebuild costs up more than the extra floor area suggests."},{"type":"preference","content":"When I cannot rely on an old valuation, I prefer to ask for a fresh rebuild estimate rather than work from market value, because the cost to reinstate the building is usually the right figure for claim triage."},{"type":"observation","content":"When an extension is detached from the main house or built over a garage, I check whether services, foundations, and external finishes now make the reinstatement more complex, since hidden building work can matter as much as visible space."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the extension was added several years ago, I assume the rebuild cost may have drifted further out of date, so I look for signs of inflation, planning conditions, and any later alterations that were never added to the sum insured."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the claim damage is localised to the extension, I still test whether the extension is integral to the structure, because a partial repair can trigger matching issues, scaffolding, or making-good to adjoining areas."},{"type":"preference","content":"When there is a loft conversion, conservatory replacement, or rear extension all on the same property, I prefer to ask for a simple room-by-room description, as that helps me judge whether the rebuild cost should be uplifted in stages."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the rebuild figure looks low for a property with an extension, I check for omissions like upgraded electricals, plumbing reroutes, insulation, and decoration, because these often sit outside the member's first estimate but still count in reinstatement."},{"type":"fact","content":"When uncertainty remains, I cap my delegated decision at the most conservative repair route and flag the case for further validation, because underestimating rebuild cost after an extension can affect settlement and future adequacy of cover."}]}
